titre: A Cake Can Raise Blood Sugar Less Than a Potato
accroche: In 1981, in Toronto, a team measures the real effect of 62 foods on blood sugar, and overturns an assumption used for decades.
contenu_vulgarise:
Since the 1950s, people with diabetes had been taught to plan meals using carbohydrate exchange lists: a hundred grams of potatoes, a certain amount of bread, a certain amount of lentils, all interchangeable as long as the carbohydrate weight matched. The idea seemed reasonable: a gram of carbohydrate is a gram of carbohydrate, whatever food carries it.

## An Assumption No One Had Really Measured

In 1981, David Jenkins's team at the University of Toronto decides to test this assumption by actually measuring it. They give small groups of five to ten fasting volunteers sixty-two common foods and sugars, each in a quantity providing the same amount of available carbohydrate, then track their blood sugar for two hours and compare the area under the curve to the one produced by the same amount of pure glucose. If the exchange lists were right, every food should produce roughly the same curve. That's not what happens. Root vegetables come out on top, with an average response of 70% of glucose's; breakfast cereals follow at 65%; dairy products drop to 35%; dried legumes, to just 31%. Foods high in fat or protein raise blood sugar more slowly, whatever their carbohydrate weight, while their fiber or sugar content, on its own, predicts very little.

## The Shift

The practical consequence reaches well beyond diabetes. A chocolate cake, because it contains fat that slows absorption, ends up with a lower glycemic index than a boiled potato or a bowl of white rice, two foods that intuition nonetheless files on the sensible side of the plate. The exchange lists couldn't see this difference, because they measured what went into the food, never what the body did with it once digested. The glycemic index shifted the question asked of a food: no longer how much carbohydrate it contains, but how fast that carbohydrate reaches the bloodstream. Two identical carbohydrates on a label can behave very differently once swallowed, and that is exactly what the label never says. A well-designed exchange list should have measured digesting bodies, not just food sitting on a scale.

repere.texte: Across 62 foods tested in 1981, vegetables produced an average glycemic response of 70% (± 5) of pure glucose's, breakfast cereals 65% (± 5), dairy products 35% (± 1), and dried legumes 31% (± 3), at equal carbohydrate mass.
repere.source: Jenkins, D.J., Wolever, T.M., Taylor, R.H. et al., American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 1981, 34(3):362-366

carte.punch: A chocolate cake can raise blood sugar less than a potato.
carte.idee: In 1981, a Toronto team measures for the first time the real effect of 62 foods on blood sugar, at equal carbohydrate amounts. Vegetables and breakfast cereals raise blood sugar far more than dried legumes do, contradicting the idea that all carbohydrates are equal.

quiz.question: According to the 1981 study, why can two foods containing the same amount of carbohydrate have very different effects on blood sugar?
choix: Because not all the study's volunteers were fasting before the measurements
Because only the added sugar content determines how fast glucose is absorbed
Because legumes actually contain more carbohydrate than previously thought
Because other components of the food, such as fat or protein, slow down glucose absorption
quiz.explication: The study shows that fat and protein content is linked to a slower rise in blood sugar, while sugar or fiber content, on its own, isn't enough to explain it. The volunteers were fasting, a condition of the protocol, and the issue isn't the carbohydrate content of legumes, but their effect on blood sugar at an equal amount.
